entries.name: Curtis Lab
entries.focus: The lab works on cancer systems biology and combines experimental, computational and AI methods to improve cancer diagnosis, treatment and early detection. Its main themes are modeling how tumors evolve, linking genetic changes to malignant traits, and developing biomarkers to guide treatment decisions. Current members work on early cancer evolution (for example Barrett's esophagus and intestinal metaplasia), tissue ecology in ER+ breast cancer using single-cell spatial transcriptomics, and AI/ML for spatial multiomics and computational pathology. I could not open the individual research pages, so the specific methods listed here come from the main page and the members' own focus descriptions.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps strongly on cancer genomics, computational and ML methods, and single-cell and spatial omics. Structural variants and bulk WGS or transcriptome work are less clearly emphasized on the pages I could access. The lab is in the US, so the student may need a visa.

flags: The old Stanford lab page (med.stanford.edu/curtislab) says the lab moved to curtis-lab.com, so the new site is the current one.
No email addresses are published on the members page.
The members page does not give a date or years in program, so I could not tell how current it is.

The page lists clinical fellows (Marni McClure, Audris Chiang, Colin Bergstrom, Zach Ziheng Xu), a post-baccalaureate researcher (Jimmy Zhang) and a medical student (Sophia Pribus). I left them out as not postdocs or PhD students.

entries.name: Goodarzi Lab
entries.focus: The lab pairs experimental biology with computational methods to study human disease at the molecular level, mainly metastatic cancer and neurodegenerative disease. Its computational work includes AI/ML models for genomics. A second thread is cancer evolution and tumour-environment interactions. A third is post-transcriptional gene regulation, including RNA biology in metastasis. The lab recruits computational biology, RNA biology and cancer postdocs, and takes students from UCSF's Tetrad, BMS, BMI and IPQB programs.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps with the student's interests in cancer genomics and ML methods for genomics, but its emphasis is RNA regulation and wet-lab/AI work. Structural variants, somatic mutation analysis and WGS are not evident themes, and the US location would likely need a visa.

flags: The PI is dual-affiliated: Arc Core Investigator since 2023 and still at UCSF, so this is not a full move. goodarzilab.ucsf.edu/people redirects to the Arc homepage.

entries.name: Alexandrov Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies mutational signatures, which are the patterns of somatic mutation left in genomes by endogenous and environmental processes. They develop computational methods to find and attribute these signatures across single-base substitutions, indels, copy number and structural variation. They apply these methods to large cancer whole-genome and exome cohorts and to normal tissues, including clonal hematopoiesis and exposure-related mutagenesis. Other work includes duplex sequencing to detect rare mutations, APOBEC mutagenesis, machine learning integration, deep learning on histopathology slides, and signature-based biomarkers for therapy and tumour evolution.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's interests in cancer whole-genome sequencing, somatic mutation and structural variant analysis, and computational and ML methods. There is little single-cell or spatial omics work, and a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.name: Getz Lab
entries.focus: The lab does cancer genome analysis. It looks for somatic events that drive cancer or resistance to therapy, and for germline risk variants. It uses these to define disease subtypes and link them to clinical outcomes. It builds analysis tools and pipelines for large national and international cancer genome projects, and it has a large engineering and staff-scientist group alongside its trainees. Current work, from the roster and 2026 job postings, includes multiple myeloma initiation, progression and relapse, spatial multi-omics, structural variation patterns, and immunotherapy and CAR-T resistance in lymphoma, using whole-genome/exome and transcriptome sequencing and statistical and machine-learning models.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps strongly on cancer WGS/transcriptome analysis, somatic mutation and structural variant methods, ML, and spatial omics. The main hurdle is that a US visa would be needed.

entries.name: Ding Lab
entries.focus: The lab works on computational cancer genomics. It integrates large-scale multi-omic data, including whole-genome and exome sequencing, RNA-seq, proteomics, single-cell and single-nucleus sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics and proteomics. It is a long-standing member of consortium efforts such as TCGA and CPTAC. It also works on cellular senescence and aging (SenNet), using organoid, PDX and mouse models together with imaging and AI-based computational pathology. The lab's code is on GitHub (ding-lab). entries.name: Ideker Lab
entries.focus: The lab aims to build an AI-driven model of the cell that can turn a patient's data into precision diagnosis and treatment. Its main approach is mapping cellular and disease networks, using protein-interaction and multi-scale cell-structure maps. It has also mapped genetic interactions, including synthetic-lethal maps made with CRISPR/Cas9. It develops the Cytoscape network analysis software and leads large programs: the Cancer Cell Map Initiative, the NIH Bridge2AI Cell Maps for AI project, and the ARPA-H ADAPT 'digital tumors' project for precision oncology. Methods combine interpretable machine learning on biological hierarchies, tumour genomics and imaging, and network biology.

entries.department_hint: Innovation Investigator, Arc Institute; Assistant Professor of Chemical Engineering, Stanford
entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning models of biological sequence and evolution, with the aim of aligning biological AI with human good. It studies how the immune system balances short-term protection with long-term adaptability, in order to inform more robust therapeutics. It also builds evolutionary and generative genome language models, such as Evo 2, to design new proteins, genes, antibodies and bacteriophage genomes. A third area is safe biological AI: generative models that help researchers counter harmful biology. The work is mostly computational and focuses on model development and design, not on cancer or clinical genomics.

entries.name: Palotie Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the genetic basis of common neurological, neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric diseases, including migraine, epilepsy and schizophrenia, along with their comorbidities and some cardiovascular traits. It uses clinical and population samples from the Finnish founder population. Its methods are genome-wide association studies, sequencing studies, and family-based designs. The group exploits population bottlenecks to find low-frequency and rare variants. Palotie is also Scientific Director/Chief Scientific Officer of the FinnGen biobank-scale project. The group's published description does not mention cancer.

entries.name: Klein Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops technologies and computational methods to study how cells make fate decisions in development and disease. It is known for high-throughput single-cell transcriptomics (inDrop) and for computational analysis of cell state and lineage dynamics. Current work includes semi-permeable CAGE capsules for multi-step single-cell genomic analysis and live-cell functional screening, and genomics tools for mapping the niche and signaling landscapes that determine stem-cell self-renewal and fate. It also covers microbial functional genomics and perturbational transcriptomics in bacteria, cross-species transcriptomics, and single-cell tracking of differentiation.

entries.name: Segre Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops and applies statistical and computational methods that combine large-scale human genetics (GWAS and sequencing) with functional genomics and systems biology. The aim is to identify causal genes, regulatory variants and cell types in common eye diseases, mainly primary open-angle glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy. Methods include eQTL integration (the PI is a GTEx core team member), single-cell RNA-seq and whole-genome sequencing from human eye tissues, and a multi-lab human eye cell atlas. Newer work uses perturbational expression profiles to find drug-repurposing opportunities. The lab studies germline genetic risk in a non-cancer disease context and does no cancer genomics.

fit.reason: The lab's computational methods and single-cell genomics overlap with the student's interests, but the lab studies germline GWAS and eye disease, not tumour sequencing, structural variants, somatic mutation or cancer, and it is in the US, so a visa may be needed.

entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning methods that combine and translate between very different types of biological data. It also builds methods that infer causal or regulatory relationships from that data. A major application is single-cell perturbation data, such as drug, knockout and overexpression screens, where the lab predicts the effects of unseen perturbations. A particular interest is how genome packing (chromatin organization) relates to gene regulation in health and disease. The lab's postdocs are co-advised with imaging, spatial and single-cell groups (Fei Chen, Xiao Wang, Paul Blainey, Ramnik Xavier, Eliezer Van Allen), so the lab touches spatial omics and some cancer-related work.

entries.name: Patel Lab
entries.focus: The group develops computational and AI methods to analyze how genetics and environment jointly shape health and disease. Core work is exposome research, including leading the NEXUS network (Network for Exposomics in the United States). They integrate multi-omics data (proteomic, regulomic, exposomic and microbiome) with real-world data such as EHRs, claims, wearables and satellite data. They also use machine learning to predict individual health trajectories (for example lung function, diabetes and brain aging). A meta-science strand studies the robustness of big-data findings, using the 'vibration of effects' approach.

entries.name: Smillie Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies host-microbiome interactions in the human gut, using cell atlases of the colon and enteric nervous system and spatial transcriptomics. A third theme is computational method development for spatial transcriptomics, covering cell-cell interaction inference and linking disease-risk genetics to cells and pathways.

entries.name: Marks Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses machine learning to interpret genetic variation and to design biological molecules. It has three areas: (1) learning the 'language of life', which uses evolutionary couplings between co-mutating amino acids to study protein and RNA structure and function; (2) predicting the effects of single and combined mutations and designing stable, functional protein sequences; and (3) viral evolution and immunology, which predicts viral escape and pathogenicity, improves immune recognition and identifies antibody targets. Current members also work on T-cell receptor and antibody models, immune repertoires, enzyme and protein dynamics, and interpretable ML for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. The lab's tagline is 'Machine learning to accelerate biology'.

entries.name: Rheinbay Lab
entries.focus: The lab identifies and functionally characterizes non-coding driver mutations in tumour whole-genome sequences. It does this mainly by developing new computational analysis methods and collaborating with experimental groups. A second theme is breast and prostate cancer genomics and epigenomics, including the FOXA1 oncogene and its regulatory-element and 3' UTR mutations. A third theme is the role of the sex chromosomes in cancer, especially loss of the Y chromosome (LOY). The lab is building specialized tools to define Y chromosome status in tumours, which is hard because the chromosome is repetitive. The PI co-led the PCAWG non-coding driver analysis of 2,658 whole genomes (Nature, 2020).

fit.reason: The lab's work on tumour whole-genome somatic mutation analysis and computational method development matches the student's core interests, but I saw no evidence of single-cell/spatial or transcriptome-focused work, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Vazquez-Garcia Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how tumours evolve across space and time, how they progress, and how they respond to therapy. Its current work centres on scalable inference methods and modelling for single-cell genomic data and in situ imaging data. A particular emphasis is on how tumours and the immune system co-evolve. The work is largely computational, combining statistical and machine-learning methods with mathematical modelling of tumour and disease evolution. This page does not describe specific cancer types or datasets, so the finer detail comes from the PI's publications, which I did not review.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's interests in computational methods and ML for cancer genomics and in single-cell and spatial omics; there is less visible emphasis on bulk WGS/transcriptome and structural-variant analysis, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods for single-cell, spatial and temporal genomics data. It applies them, with disease experts, to inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. The lab site lists its themes as data integration, spatial mapping, temporal mapping and cross-disease comparison. Current members work on spatial transcriptomics methods (including Xenium data), Bayesian machine learning, multi-omics regulatory variant prediction, and sex and individual differences in immune responses. The lab's focus is immune-mediated disease, not cancer.

entries.name: Buenrostro Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how cells acquire and reverse epigenetic changes and how those changes contribute to disease. It builds on ATAC-seq and extends it to single-cell assays (scATAC-seq, dsciATAC-seq, SHARE-seq) and to spatial genome mapping (IGS, ExIGS, slide-DNA-seq). It develops machine-learning models trained on epigenomic data to infer cell composition and function and to predict cell fate. It also studies epigenetic memory of inflammation and its link to cancer priming, and uses social-adversity models to study how stress affects the epigenome, immune and endocrine systems, and aging. A further goal is population-scale epigenomic sequencing with biobanks.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with single-cell and spatial omics and with computational and ML methods for genomics, but the lab focuses on chromatin and epigenomics, adversity and aging, with little on tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation, and a US role may need a visa.

entries.focus: The lab builds computational methods that use human genetics to understand and treat disease, with a current emphasis on diabetes and related metabolic traits. It coordinates the Knowledge Portal Network and the NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem Knowledge Center, and it is a Knowledge Provider for the NCATS Biomedical Translator.

entries.focus: The lab uses human genetics and genomics to identify genes and variants that influence common diseases and traits, especially height, weight/obesity, and the timing of puberty. Hirschhorn leads the GIANT consortium, which has identified most known common variants for human height and weight. The lab develops computational methods for GWAS, rare-variant aggregation tests, and gene and variant prioritization, and it uses biobank-scale data. Current projects also cover Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (HEDGE), diabetic kidney disease, PCOS and reproductive disorders, skeletal growth, and combined genomic and metabolomic analyses.

entries.name: Mercader Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the genetic basis of type 2 diabetes and related metabolic traits, with an emphasis on diverse ancestries to support equitable precision medicine. The PI's work includes developing and evaluating polygenic risk scores across ancestries, and studying rare and recessive variants that contribute to diabetes and its complications. The lab also integrates omics resources to interpret disease-associated variants. One example is the TIGER islet gene-expression resource, which Mercader co-led. The work is human-genomics and statistical-genetics based, with international collaborations. It does not study cancer.

entries.name: Kellis Lab
entries.focus: The lab aims to understand the mechanistic basis of human disease using computational and experimental methods. It finds and characterizes functional elements in the human genome, and it identifies the gene-regulatory circuits that control them. entries.name: Hemberg Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational and statistical methods for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. Current methods work covers spatial statistics for tissue organisation, a next-generation Harmony for batch correction that scales to tens of millions of cells, and Scotia, which infers cell-cell communication from spatial data. Collaborative applications include pancreatic cancer treatment resistance (Hwang lab), CAR T-cell response in solid tumours, influenza vaccine response, and perianal fistulizing disease. The lab was at the Wellcome Sanger Institute from 2014 to 2021.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's interest in computational methods and single-cell/spatial omics in cancer (pancreatic cancer, liquid-biopsy RNA, CAR-T tumours), but there is little focus on whole-genome sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutation calling.

entries.name: Baym Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies microbial evolution through experiment, computation and theory. entries.name: Talkowski Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how genomic variation, especially structural variation (SV), contributes to neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism. They build population-scale SV resources, including the Structural Variation Atlas, the GATK-SV pipeline, and long-read gnomAD, and map complex genomic rearrangements. They run large gene-discovery and disease-association studies in autism and related neurodevelopmental disorders, including rare-disease and bipolar cohorts. They use cellular and functional modeling (iPSC-derived neural models, high-throughput variant-to-function assays, long-read RNA-seq and splicing) to interpret variants. They also work on translational prenatal and pediatric genomic diagnostics.

entries.name: Udler Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses human genetics to improve diagnosis and treatment of diabetes and metabolic disease. It builds partitioned polygenic scores and clusters genetic loci into mechanism-specific groups to explain heterogeneity in type 2 diabetes. A 2024 Nature Medicine paper from the lab did this in more than 1.4 million people across ancestries. It also leads MGH recruitment for the RADIANT study of rare and atypical diabetes, using sequencing to find new genes and variants. Data sources are large biobanks (UK Biobank, Mass General Brigham Biobank, the T2D Knowledge Portal). Methods are statistical genetics, GWAS and polygenic scores, multi-omics, and pharmacogenomics, alongside a clinical Diabetes Genetics Clinic.

fit.reason: The lab shares computational and statistical-genomics methods with the student, but it works on germline genetics of diabetes and metabolic disease rather than cancer, tumour WGS/transcriptomes, somatic or structural variants, or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Rigollet Lab
entries.focus: The group works at the interface of statistics, machine learning and optimization, with a focus on high-dimensional statistical methods. One theme models transformers as interacting particle systems, where self-attention acts as a velocity field that moves tokens, and studies the resulting clustering behaviour. A second theme applies Wasserstein gradient flows and optimal transport to statistics and ML, including particle-based variational inference and nonparametric maximum likelihood. A third theme applies transformers and probability-measure methods to biological data, treating cell populations as probability measures, for example to predict treatment response in patient-derived organoids. The group does this work with the Schmidt Center at the Broad Institute and is recruiting postdocs on maths-biology and genomics.

Because high-throughput measurements destroy cells, it engineers cells that record their lineage and signaling histories in their own DNA, and it develops cell barcoding with in situ readout alongside transcriptomes. It also uses directed viral evolution for gene delivery, and gastruloid and organoid models of early human development. Analysis relies on differential geometry, machine learning, population genetics and stochastic processes, including reconstructing the origins and clonal expansion of blood cancers in individual patients.

entries.name: Naqvi Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how quantitative control of gene expression shapes development and the 'tipping points' that lead to disease. It focuses on transcription factor (TF) dosage. It uses chemical-genetic approaches to modulate TF levels in fine increments in human stem cells and their derived cell types, such as neural crest. The lab pairs these perturbations with functional genomics and builds predictive computational and machine learning models of the molecular, cellular and morphological effects. The goal is to identify the regulatory elements, genes and cell states most sensitive to dosage changes. The PI's earlier work covered cis-regulatory divergence between human and chimpanzee, and sex-biased gene expression in mammals.

The lab does not appear to focus on cancer genomics or sequencing-based variant calling.

entries.name: Rothenberg Lab
entries.department_hint: Biology and Biological Engineering (gene regulatory network modelling; T-cell development)
entries.focus: The lab studies how hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells become T lymphocytes. It looks at the transcription factors and signalling events that switch on T-lineage genes and suppress alternative fates, and at what separates reversible activation of the T-cell program from irreversible commitment. Methods include in vitro precursor differentiation systems, single-cell profiling of developmental states, retroviral perturbation, and genome-wide analysis of transcription factor binding against changing chromatin. Further themes are gene regulatory network modelling, variation that may predispose to autoimmunity, and the evolutionary origins of T, B and innate lymphocyte programs in basal vertebrates.

fit.reason: The lab does use single-cell and genome-wide computational methods and gene regulatory network modelling, but it works on normal T-cell development, not cancer genomics, tumour WGS/transcriptome sequencing or structural variant and somatic mutation analysis.

entries.focus: The lab studies biomolecular computation, mainly by building computing systems out of DNA. Its topics include algorithmic self-assembly of DNA tiles and origami, and enzyme-free DNA strand displacement circuits. Other topics are in vitro biochemical circuits and chemical reaction networks, DNA-based molecular robotics, and molecular self-replication and evolution. The group also works on multistranded nucleic acid kinetics, sequence design, fault-tolerant molecular computing, and more recently phase separation and pattern formation. Methods combine theory and simulation with wet-lab DNA nanotechnology experiments.

entries.focus: The lab's tagline is "Making Sense of Biological Designs". entries.name: Guttman Lab
entries.department_hint: Biology and Biological Engineering (experimental plus computational genomics)
entries.focus: The lab studies how long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) regulate gene expression and organize the nucleus in 3D. A major model is Xist and X-chromosome silencing. Xist finds its targets through 3D proximity, spreads by remodeling X-chromosome structure, and recruits SHARP/SMRT/HDAC3 to exclude RNA Polymerase II. The lab also proposes a 'seed, bind, recruit' model, in which hundreds of ncRNAs form nuclear compartments that concentrate RNA-binding proteins, and it examines the role of phase separation. Methods include SPRITE (mapping RNA, DNA and protein assemblies in 3D at single-molecule resolution), RNA-protein interaction profiling, CRISPRi screens, single-cell transcriptomics, and microscopy. Other work covers SARS-CoV-2 protein interactions with host RNAs.

fit.reason: This is mostly experimental RNA and nuclear-architecture biology, with some single-cell and genomic method development. It has little cancer genomics, tumour WGS, structural-variant or somatic-mutation work, so overlap with the student's interests is limited, and it would involve a US visa.

entries.focus: The lab develops statistical methods for high-throughput genomic data, with robust estimation, high-dimensional inference, hypothesis testing and multivariate data integration. Past work includes cortical neuron classification, sorghum drought epigenomics, and tumour mutation spectra with UCSF and OHSU collaborators.

entries.name: O'Connor Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and mathematical methods to characterize the genetic architecture of common diseases and traits. One thread quantifies how common and rare variants contribute to disease risk, how natural selection shapes that architecture, and how functional annotations can be integrated. This includes work on autism and forecasts of what rare-variant association studies will find at larger sample sizes. A second thread builds methods that use genealogical relatedness (shared haplotypes from common ancestors). It includes a genealogical representation of the linkage disequilibrium (LD) matrix that speeds up calculations such as heritability partitioning, and a similar representation for genotype data. The work is population-genetic and statistical, centred on GWAS and rare-variant data. It does not cover tumour sequencing, somatic mutation, or single-cell and spatial omics.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational and statistical methods for genomics, but it works on germline common and rare variants in complex traits. It does no cancer, somatic, structural-variant, or single-cell and spatial work, and a US role may need a visa.

entries.name: Baym Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies microbial evolution through experiment, computation and theory. A central topic is how mobile genetic elements (plasmids, transposons, prophages) interact with each other and with their bacterial hosts. The lab also asks how selection at the level of the cell, between cells and across populations drives rapid adaptation, with antibiotic resistance as a recurring theme. Methods include synthetic lab evolution systems, large-scale analysis of clinical and environmental sequencing data, and new technologies.

entries.name: Gehlenborg Lab (HIDIVE)
entries.focus: The lab builds interactive visualization and analysis tools that help scientists and clinicians explore complex biomedical data. Its open-source software includes HiGlass (genome/Hi-C browsing), Gosling (a grammar for genomics visualization), and Vitessce (single-cell and spatial data). Application areas include cancer genomics (for example TCGA data visualization), epigenomics and 3D genome organization, and single-cell and spatial atlases such as HuBMAP, SenNet and KPMP. Methods combine human-computer interaction, visualization research, and software engineering for reproducible, collaborative data analysis.

fit.reason: Single-cell/spatial omics and cancer genomics visualization overlap loosely, but the lab does visualization and HCI tooling rather than tumour WGS, structural variant calling or ML for genomics, and no PhD students are listed.

entries.name: Rajpurkar Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds medical AI that reasons from evidence, tests it before it is trusted, and teaches it to assist clinicians. Its clinical reasoning work covers AI that reads scans and records the way specialists do, and ties its answers to evidence. Its testing work evaluates AI through simulated patient conversations, hospital-scale simulation, and work alongside clinicians. A third line is assistive robotics, where robots help clinicians with their hands while the clinician stays in control. The lab mixes computer scientists and clinicians, and the work centres on medical imaging and clinical-record AI.

fit.reason: The lab works on clinical and imaging AI, not cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics. The only overlap is general machine-learning methods, and a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.name: Sunyaev Lab
entries.focus: The lab is a computational genomics group that studies genetic variation: how mutations arise, how variants alter molecular function and structure, and how selection shapes variation in populations. Population genetics is used as a tool to study evolution and to understand how complex traits and their allelic architecture are maintained. Members work on mutagenesis and DNA repair, mutation-rate maps, negative selection and genetic dominance, and GWAS and rare-variant analysis. The lab also develops statistical and machine-learning methods for sequencing studies, such as the PolyPhen-2 variant-effect predictor. It has smaller cancer genomics projects, including tumour progression modelling with the Van Allen lab. The lab is mostly population-genetic and germline-focused rather than tumour-sequencing-focused.

entries.name: Keating Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how proteins bind each other in eukaryotic signaling, and it combines computational modeling with experiments to do so. A major thread is Bcl-2 family proteins that control apoptosis. Structure-based and machine-learning models predict BH3 motif binding, and these models have produced peptide reagents for assessing programmed cell death in cancer cells. Newer projects cover short linear motif recognition by domains such as TRAF, EVH1 and the E3 ligase Itch. The lab also designs peptide binders and inhibitors, including cyclotides and conformationally pre-organized peptides. Methods include yeast surface display, photo-crosslinking, and machine learning for sequence–structure–energy landscapes.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in machine learning methods and touches cancer biology through apoptosis, but it works on protein structure and peptide design, not genomics, sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Bryson Lab
entries.focus: The lab combines immunoengineering, molecular microbiology, and synthetic and systems biology to design new therapeutics for infectious disease. Its main focus is Mycobacterium tuberculosis and the role of the human innate immune system, especially macrophages, in controlling infection. It builds tools to study infection from single cells to whole infected animals, using quantitative modeling with classical microbiology and immunology methods. The two central questions are which macrophage processes kill bacteria and how the bacteria resist them, and how macrophage plasticity can be manipulated to program function. The long-term goal is to inform TB vaccine design.

fit.reason: The lab's computational and systems-biology work on host-pathogen immunology overlaps only loosely with the student's cancer genomics, structural variant and tumour sequencing interests, and it is a US lab that would need a visa.

entries.name: Coley Research Group
entries.focus: The group works at the intersection of AI and chemistry. It builds machine learning models of how molecules behave, interact and react, and uses them to design new molecules, with an emphasis on therapeutic discovery. Topics include computer-aided synthesis planning and retrosynthesis, reaction outcome and mechanism prediction, generative models for small-molecule and 3D structure-based drug design, and structure elucidation from mass spectrometry and metabolomics data. Most of the work is computational. The group also uses laboratory automation and high-throughput experimentation to test hypotheses and generate data, for example in catalyst design and nanoparticle cancer therapeutics.

entries.name: Page Lab
entries.focus: The Page lab studies how genetic differences between males and females arise and what they mean for biology and medicine, both inside and outside the reproductive tract. It uses comparative, evolutionary, developmental and clinical approaches. The lab sequenced the sex chromosomes of eight mammals and chicken, and found Y-linked genes with X-linked counterparts that are expressed throughout the body. It now studies how XX versus XY chromosome makeup shapes genome-wide sex differences in gene expression and disease, using genomic, proteomic and epigenetic profiling. It also develops methods for high-quality sequencing of complex genomic regions, and uses mouse models of germ cell development, with implications for infertility and germ cell cancers.

fit.reason: The lab is strong in genomics and computational analysis, but its focus is sex-chromosome biology and germ cells, not cancer genomics, structural variants in tumours or single-cell/spatial cancer omics (only a minor link through germ cell cancers). Joining would also need a US visa.

entries.focus: The lab studies the 3D organization of the genome. A central topic is loop extrusion by SMC complexes such as cohesin and condensin, and how it shapes chromosome folding, enhancer-promoter communication and DNA repair. The lab also builds computational tools, including Bayesian inference of loop extrusion and the machine-learning tool Manta.

entries.name: Greener Group (biomolecular simulation / force fields)
entries.focus: The group works on improving molecular dynamics force fields, which describe how atoms interact. Its main targets are disordered proteins and protein aggregation. One approach trains fast molecular mechanics force fields with graph neural networks, using quantum mechanics and experimental data, to build a reproducible universal force field for biologically relevant molecules. A second approach develops machine learning interatomic potentials that are fast enough for biomolecular simulation, using simpler models and GPU programming. The long-term aim is to simulate enzyme reactions. Related work covers protein design with molecular simulation, free energy methods and protein folding.

entries.focus: The group develops image-processing methods for atomic-resolution structure determination by cryo-EM and cryo-ET. These are implemented in the open-source software RELION. Their work shows that one protein can adopt many amyloid folds; for example, tau forms filaments in more than 20 diseases, and different folds characterise different diseases. Current work includes in vitro assembly of amyloids that replicate brain-derived folds, tau and alpha-synuclein aggregation, and machine-learning methods for cryo-ET and protein design.

Model systems are humans, dogs and yeast.

entries.focus: The lab studies how RNA structural dynamics govern RNA-protein binding and function. This is done with computational and experimental methods, both in vitro and in cells. Current work centres on viral RNAs, especially quantitative modelling of how the HIV Gag polyprotein binds and oligomerizes on the HIV 5'-leader RNA to start genome packaging. A second theme is dynamics-based RNA drug targeting, which seeks rare, low-populated RNA conformations that small molecules could target. Methods include high-throughput mutational analysis of thousands of RNA variants, NMR, molecular dynamics, RNA structure prediction, and virtual screening with AutoDock.

fit.reason: The lab does RNA structural biology and antiviral drug discovery, with essentially no overlap with cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics. The only link is a general computational/high-throughput flavour.

entries.focus: The lab combines computational and experimental methods to study how tissues are cellularly organized. entries.name: Gentles Lab
entries.focus: The Gentles lab is a computational biology group that analyses large patient cohorts to study human health and disease, mainly cancer and neurodegeneration. A major theme is pan-cancer discovery of prognostic cell types and states. The lab uses CIBERSORTx deconvolution of bulk expression, single-cell RNA-seq and genomic atlases, and it studies how spatial cell organisation shapes tissue behaviour. Another theme is lymph nodes and metastasis, where genomic data and CODEX imaging are used to ask how immune cells come to tolerate migrated tumour cells (Stanford Center for Cancer Systems Biology). A third theme looks for pathways shared between cancer and neurodegeneration, including Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia, in collaboration with the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute.

fit.reason: Single-cell/spatial omics in cancer and computational methods overlap well with the student's interests, but the lab works mainly on expression deconvolution and cohort-level analysis rather than tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation calling, and a US role would need a visa.

entries.name: Laboratory of Evolutionary Design
entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning methods for understanding and designing proteins and genomes. It is best known for the Evo biological foundation model, which does sequence modeling and design from the molecular scale to the genome scale. entries.name: Alsentzer Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning and natural language processing methods that support clinical decision-making and broaden access to high-quality healthcare. One theme integrates domain knowledge by combining structured biomedical sources such as knowledge graphs with unstructured clinical text. entries.name: Pritchard Lab
entries.focus: The lab is mainly computational. It works on statistical genetics, population genetics and ML-based genomics, and has close ties to wet-lab groups. A major theme is linking GWAS and rare-variant results to causal mechanisms, which it calls 'Trait Causal Models'. These models combine genome-scale Perturb-seq and single-cell omics with the omnigenic 'core gene' and trans-regulatory network view of heritability. The work is applied mainly to T cells and immune traits, in collaboration with Alex Marson's lab, and to red blood cell traits. Other work covers QTL mapping and splicing (LeafCutter, WASP), trans-regulation by CRISPR perturbation, population structure and ancient DNA (STRUCTURE, TreeMix), polygenic adaptation and selection, recombination, and the human mutation spectrum.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational and ML methods and single-cell work, but it focuses on human complex-trait genetics, population genetics and T-cell regulation. It does little tumour WGS or structural-variant work; the main cancer link is Alvina Adimoelja's population genetics

entries.name: Palacios Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical methods for complex random processes, using Bayesian nonparametrics, stochastic processes, probabilistic AI and computational statistics. A core theme is coalescent-based inference of population-size dynamics and phylogenetic tree inference, including flexible machine-learning and variational models for distributions over tree topologies. Applications are evolutionary dynamics in population genetics and infectious disease (epidemiology and pathogen phylodynamics). Cancer applications include single-cell lineage tracing.

fit.reason: The lab is statistical-methods-heavy, centred on phylogenetics and epidemiology. Its only overlap with the student's cancer genomics, structural variant and sequencing interests is the computational-methods angle and a minor single-cell lineage-tracing thread. It does no tumour WGS or SV work.

entries.name: Salzman Lab
entries.focus: The lab treats genomic data as a statistical signal-processing problem. It uses statistics, machine learning and deep learning for biological discovery, with stated interests in splicing, cancer and microbes. A flagship method is SPLASH (and the related NOMAD framework), a reference-free, annotation-free statistical approach that finds sequence variation directly in raw sequencing reads. It is applied to alternative splicing, RNA editing, V(D)J-like diversity, microbial and viral variation, and predictive phenotype models. Cancer-related work includes gene-fusion and circular RNA detection and validation, and new statistical methods for spatial and single-cell sequencing data such as MERFISH isoform analysis.

entries.name: Huang Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how bacterial cells and microbial communities are organized and function. I did not open the lab's research page, so this summary comes from general knowledge of the lab and is not verified against the site. Its work covers bacterial cell shape, growth and cell-wall mechanics, using quantitative imaging, biophysical modelling and computation. A second theme is the human gut microbiome: community assembly, antibiotic response and the effects of the microbiome on host physiology. Methods include microscopy, high-throughput culturing and sequencing (for example 16S and metagenomics), and mathematical and machine-learning models.

fit.reason: The lab's computational and sequencing-based microbiome work gives some methods overlap, but it does not cover cancer genomics, structural variants, somatic mutations, tumour sequencing or single-cell/spatial omics in cancer.

entries.name: Steinmetz Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops genomics technologies and uses them to study how genetic variation shapes complex traits, gene regulation and inherited disease. Methods include high-throughput CRISPR genome editing and screens that link genotype to phenotype, single-cell RNA-seq and multi-omics, and enhancer-gene mapping. Applied work covers precision health (dilated cardiomyopathy, immune disorders, mitochondrial disease; the EMBL page also mentions cancer) and the Sc2.0 synthetic yeast genome project. The long-term goal is to assign a function to every nucleotide in the human genome.

fit.reason: The lab has method overlap through single-cell omics, genome-scale functional genomics and computational analysis, but it centres on yeast and human variant function and cardiomyopathy rather than cancer genomics, tumour WGS or structural variants, and any role would need a US visa.

entries.name: Rivas Lab
entries.focus: The lab does population-scale human genetics and genomics, using biobank genotype, exome and phenotype data. Recent work includes a meta-regression of ultra-rare variants from epilepsy exome sequencing (about 21k cases and 33k controls), and LLM-informed literature priors for re-analysing exome results in schizophrenia, autism, epilepsy, IBD and obesity. The lab also develops statistical and machine-learning methods, such as the univariate guided lasso for genome-wide risk prediction in biobanks. Newer directions include AI dashboards for tumour boards, algorithms for optimising clinical trials, and quantum computing algorithms for human genetics.

entries.name: Stanford Center for Biomedical Informatics Research (BMIR)
entries.focus: The lab works on semantic technology for biomedical science: ontologies, metadata, and data stewardship that make research data FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable). Its main projects are CEDAR (the Center for Expanded Data Annotation and Retrieval, which builds tools for authoring standards-based metadata for experimental datasets), the National Center for Biomedical Ontology (BioPortal), and the Protégé ontology editor. It also does work on intelligent systems and knowledge-based decision support. The methods are mostly knowledge engineering, ontology and semantic-web engineering, and metadata quality and recommendation. This is data-infrastructure and informatics work, not genomics or omics analysis.

fit.reason: The lab works on ontologies and metadata infrastructure and does not do cancer genomics, structural variant analysis, sequencing analysis or single-cell/spatial omics. The overlap is limited to data annotation standards that could be useful for genomics datasets.

entries.name: Covert Lab
entries.focus: The lab does systems biology, with a focus on host-pathogen interactions and the innate immune system. One main area is whole-cell computational modeling, which integrates known information about each gene and molecule to predict cell behavior. The lab reported its first such model in 2012. The other main area is live-cell microscopy of immune signaling, using a live-cell kinase reporter and deep learning to analyze microscopy images. Together these methods trace a cell's response from the initial stimulus, through signaling pathways, to genome-wide changes in gene expression.

fit.reason: The lab is computational and uses deep learning and single-cell live imaging, but it studies immune signaling and whole-cell models, not cancer genomics, tumour WGS/transcriptome sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutations.

entries.name: Snyder Lab
entries.focus: The lab maps transcription factor binding and regulatory networks in the noncoding genome. It applies this to iPSC differentiation and to metabolism, cancer, inflammation and autism. It studies human variation, especially structural variants and differences in regulatory information, and links them to SNPs. Its integrative personal omics profiling (iPOP) work follows genomes, transcriptomes, proteomes, metabolomes, cytokines, immune cells and the microbiome over time in a cohort of more than 100 people. It also uses wearable-device monitoring for early detection of illness. Genome-mapping pipelines are used to find causal mutations in undiagnosed disease, and DNA methylation and chromatin are studied in autism and cancer.

entries.name: Rusu Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops AI and machine learning methods that combine radiology and pathology imaging to characterise cancer, mainly prostate cancer on MRI. It also works on breast cancer and some non-oncologic applications. Methods include deep learning, radiology-pathology image registration and fusion, computer vision, and multimodal analytics. fit.reason: The overlap is limited to cancer and machine learning; the lab works on imaging AI (MRI and histopathology), not on genomics, structural variants, or sequencing-based single-cell and spatial omics.

entries.name: Daneshjou Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops and evaluates AI systems for biomedicine and healthcare, with a strong emphasis on dermatology. A major theme is bias and fairness in AI. Examples are the performance gaps of dermatology algorithms on darker skin tones and the gender and racial biases of large language models. The lab also works on vision-language models and LLMs for clinical tasks, such as dermatology clinical-trial recruitment and retention, and on skin-tone representation in AI models. The PI is a board-certified dermatologist and physician-scientist with a PhD in Genetics from Russ Altman's group. Her work links clinical AI, pharmacogenomics and precision health. It is clinical-AI and image/text oriented, not genomics-sequencing oriented.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in machine-learning methods, but its work is clinical AI, LLMs and dermatology imaging, with no cancer genomics, structural variants, WGS/transcriptome analysis or single-cell/spatial omics in the sources I saw. A US role would also need a visa.

It combines computation (transformers, neural ODEs, diffusion models) with experiments (metabolic-labeling scRNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, Perturb-seq, lineage tracing). The aim is predictive, differentiable models of cell states under perturbation. The lab is known for the software Monocle 2/3, Dynamo and Spateo, and is now building AI-native platforms (PantheonOS, Bio-Babel).

fit.reason: The lab's single-cell, spatial omics and ML-for-genomics methods overlap with the student's computational interests, but its focus is developmental biology and the heart rather than cancer genomics, tumour WGS or structural variants. The student would also likely need a US visa.

The work is germline, psychiatric and population-based, and the group releases its own software tools.

entries.focus: The lab studies somatic evolution using cancer as a model. A UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship funds work on the mutational processes and spatial context of tumour dormancy.

They study how DNA sequence and chromatin shape recombination hotspots and how recombination relates to fertility and health, using single-cell chromatin accessibility and expression data from meiosis plus lab-based experiments. A second theme is fine-scale population structure, migration and demographic history, including genotype imputation and phasing for large cohorts such as Genomics England's 100,000 Genomes Project, and genealogy-based inference (Relate) for ancient genomes. Newer work covers GWAS in stratified cohorts and the genetic architecture of extreme or unexpected phenotypes, using Bayesian and machine-learning approaches.

entries.focus: The lab aims to build artificially intelligent, mechanistic models of cancer and neurodegenerative disease that turn patient data into precision diagnosis and treatment. entries.focus: The group studies the diversity, regulation and evolution of cell types across the tree of life, using comparative regulatory genomics. entries.name: Martin Group
entries.focus: The Martin Group is a medical genomics group. It analyses large-scale genetic and electronic health record data to study the genetic architecture of rare and common diseases and quantitative traits. Its main focus is neurodevelopment and the pre-, peri- and neonatal period. Current projects include pregnancy loss, cell-free fetal DNA, fetal growth restriction and neonatal complications of premature birth. Related work covers fine-scale population structure, populations with high parental relatedness (consanguinity), rare recessive variants, and family-based designs using de novo variation for causal inference. The cohorts used include Genes & Health, the Deciphering Developmental Disorders (DDD) study and Genomics England.

entries.focus: The group studies somatic evolution: how mutations accumulate in healthy cells throughout life, and how that shapes cancer, ageing and other diseases. They chart somatic mutation and clonal selection across healthy human tissues, which bears on early cancer detection. They also study somatic mutation in non-human species. Methods combine ultra-accurate duplex sequencing (NanoSeq), laser-capture microscopy with genome sequencing, and computational methods such as dN/dS-based quantification of selection and cancer-gene discovery.

entries.focus: The group studies speciation and evolutionary genomics, with a focus on how hybridisation (interbreeding) and chromosomal rearrangements drive rapid speciation and adaptation. Main study systems are Lake Victoria and other African cichlids, Heliconius and ithomiine butterflies, and several Darwin Tree of Life taxa (beetles, wall lizards, spiders). Methods are comparative population and phylogenomics on whole genomes, plus analysis of chromosome fusions and fissions, sex chromosomes and colour-pattern genetics. Fieldwork and sampling feed the genomic work. The research is evolutionary and ecological. It has no cancer or clinical component.

entries.name: Corander Group
entries.focus: The group works on microbial evolution and transmission modelling, statistical machine learning, population genomics and inference algorithms. Its main application is large-scale genomic surveillance of bacterial pathogens. It has built methods for bacterial population structure (BAPS, hierBAPS, fastbaps) and for bacterial GWAS and GWES (SEER, pyseer, SpydrPick, SuperDCA). It also coordinates ELFI, a software package for likelihood-free inference. Current staff topics include antimicrobial resistance, vaccine impact and microbial epidemiology. Nothing found points to cancer or human genomics.

fit.reason: The group's computational and statistical machine-learning methods for genomics overlap with the student's methods interest, but its focus is bacterial population genomics, with no cancer, structural-variant, somatic-mutation, or single-cell/spatial work.

entries.name: Taipale Group
entries.focus: The group studies how DNA sequence determines when and where genes are expressed, and how tissues and organisms regulate their growth. It combines high-throughput wet-lab experiments, synthetic genomes, DNA sequencing, computation and AI. Methods include biochemical measurement of DNA-binding protein affinities and machine-learning models of sequence-to-activity maps. They also include sequence-based prediction of protein structures and affinities. The group maps transcription factor binding on free and nucleosomal DNA, with and without cytosine methylation. It applies these insights to cancer genomes and GWAS data to find regulatory regions linked to heart disease, diabetes and several cancers.

fit.reason: The group's computational and ML work on regulatory sequence and its application to cancer genome mutations overlap with the student's genomics-ML and somatic mutation interests, but the focus is on TF biochemistry and regulation rather than tumour WGS/transcriptome, SVs or single-cell/spatial omics

entries.focus: The group studies somatic mutation, DNA methylation changes and clonal selection across a lifetime, and how these change with ageing and cancer. Earlier work covered blood cancer genetics, including CALR mutations in myeloproliferative neoplasms, and using genomics to personalise predictions of disease outcome. entries.name: Jaron Group
entries.focus: The group studies the evolution of unusual reproductive mechanisms. These include asexual reproduction and parent-biased (non-Mendelian) inheritance. They compare the genomes of species with non-standard reproduction against relatives that reproduce in common ways. The work is comparative and evolutionary genomics, based on genome assemblies from the Tree of Life programme.

entries.name: Blaxter Group
entries.focus: The group works on evolutionary genomics. It asks how genomic novelty arises and how opportunity and constraint shape the diversity of life. It produces high-quality reference genome assemblies for many species through the Tree of Life Programme and the Darwin Tree of Life project. Most of this work is on animals, with some on plants, fungi, protists and their bacterial symbionts. Research topics include gene and species phylogenies, horizontal gene transfer and introgression, eukaryote–bacteria and host–parasite symbioses, chromosome structure evolution, and meiofauna (tardigrades, nematodes and other Ecdysozoa). The group also studies extremophile genomics and develops assembly, validation and analysis software such as BlobToolKit.

entries.name: Jones Group
entries.focus: The group studies how mutations let normal stem cells spread through tissues, which is the first step toward cancer. Their main models are normal human skin epidermis and the oesophageal lining. Methods include deep targeted sequencing of normal human tissue, transgenic mouse models, 3D culture, gene editing, live imaging, single-cell analysis and quantitative modelling. Questions include the competitive fitness of mutant clones, positive selection of driver mutations in normal tissue, and the earliest stages of tumour development.

entries.name: Durbin Group
entries.focus: The group applies computational and mathematical methods to whole-genome sequence data. Its work covers human population history (inferring expansions, bottlenecks and separations from modern and ancient genomes) and adaptive speciation in Lake Malawi cichlids, with over 1,100 samples from more than 200 species sequenced. It also produces high-quality long-read vertebrate reference genomes for the Vertebrate Genomes Project and Darwin Tree of Life. A further strand develops efficient algorithms and software, including BWT/suffix-array tools such as bwa and the vg variation-graph package, along with pangenome and assembly methods.

entries.name: Vento-Tormo Group
entries.focus: The group studies the principles of tissue organisation. entries.name: Google DeepMind
entries.focus: DeepMind's science group builds ML models for biology. AlphaFold predicts protein structure. AlphaGenome reads up to 1 Mb of DNA sequence and predicts 11 genomic processes, including gene expression and splicing, and it scores non-coding regulatory variant effects. It matched or beat the best external models in 25 of 26 variant-effect evaluations. It is available for non-commercial research use, and over 3,000 researchers in 160 countries had used the API by January 2026. Kohli says current work covers protein function, genome interpretation, and de novo protein and enzyme design. DeepMind has also advertised student researcher placements for AI-driven cancer discovery.

fit.reason: AlphaGenome's regulatory and non-coding variant prediction overlaps with somatic mutation analysis and ML for genomics. There is no verified DeepMind work on tumour WGS, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and the roles are US/UK-based and need work authorization.

entries.name: Google Research
entries.focus: The team applies deep learning to genome sciences. It builds open-source tools and models for genomics problems and extends TensorFlow for genomics data. DeepVariant is its best-known tool. It is a CNN-based germline SNP and small-indel caller for short-read and long-read sequencing, and it has a family and cohort calling mode. The team has also released DeepSomatic for somatic variant calling in tumour sequencing, DeepConsensus for correcting PacBio long reads, and DeepPolisher for assembly polishing. Most of the work is sequencing-data variant calling and methods development, and it ships as open-source software. I did not verify any current work on single-cell or spatial omics.

fit.reason: DeepSomatic and DeepVariant match the student's interests in somatic mutation analysis, tumour sequencing and ML methods for genomics. entries.name: Amazon / AWS
entries.focus: AWS's life-science work is mostly a platform and partner business. It is not a single research lab. In April 2026 AWS launched Amazon Bio Discovery at its Life Sciences Symposium in New York. It is an agentic AI application for early-stage drug and antibody design, with a catalogue of biological foundation models that users can fine-tune on their own experimental data. Candidates can be sent to partner wet labs, such as Twist Bioscience, and the results feed back into the system. Early adopters include MSK, Bayer, the Broad Institute and Voyager Therapeutics. AWS also provides cloud infrastructure for genomics and omics pipelines to pharma and research institutes. A separate AWS, BCG and Merck platform targets clinical-trial site selection. I found no public Amazon research group on cancer genomics, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.focus: Lilly launched TuneLab in September 2025. It is an AI/ML platform that gives smaller biotechs access to drug-discovery models trained on more than $1B of Lilly research data. entries.name: Foundation Medicine
entries.focus: Foundation Medicine develops and runs comprehensive genomic profiling tests for cancer, such as FoundationOne CDx and FoundationOne Liquid CDx. These tests detect somatic alterations in tumour tissue and circulating tumour DNA: substitutions, indels, copy-number changes, rearrangements, and biomarkers such as TMB and MSI. Its Computational Discovery group is made up of computational biologists and machine learning scientists. Per a 2025 event description and a job listing, the group does early-stage research on cancer genomics, computational pathology and clinical outcomes. It works from a large clinicogenomic dataset to develop new biomarkers and diagnostics, and to support pharma partners on companion diagnostics.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with cancer genomics, somatic mutation and structural variant analysis, and ML for genomics. It is clinical panel sequencing rather than whole-genome, transcriptome or single-cell work, and a US work-authorization barrier limits access.

entries.name: Recursion
entries.focus: Recursion is a clinical-stage 'TechBio' company that runs large-scale automated experiments in wet-lab biology and applies machine learning to the results to find drugs. It uses cell imaging and other phenomics readouts, plus transcriptomics, to map how genetic and chemical perturbations change cells. It uses these maps and its ML models to pick targets and design small molecules, with oncology and rare disease among its areas. Valence Labs is its ML research group, based in Montreal (with ties to Mila) and London. It works on foundation models for virtual cells, perturbation biology and single-cell representation. I did not verify specific oncology programs or any whole-genome sequencing work.

fit.reason: Its single-cell and ML-for-biology work (Valence Labs in Montreal) overlaps with the student's computational methods and single-cell interests. Its focus on drug discovery from cell perturbations has little overlap with cancer WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis.

entries.name: Bioptimus
entries.focus: Bioptimus is a Paris-based company, founded in 2024, that builds foundation models it calls a 'world model of biology'. The models span histology, spatial and bulk transcriptomics, genomics and clinical data. H-Optimus is a pathology foundation model trained on very large numbers of whole-slide histopathology images, used for cancer grading and biomarker detection. M-Optimus, announced in December 2025, is a multimodal model that links histology, transcriptomics and clinical records across cells, tissues and patients. It is in early access with pharma partners. The STELA initiative gathers multi-institutional patient data. The Scientific Advisory Board is chaired by Sarah Teichmann.

entries.name: Inceptive
entries.focus: Inceptive describes itself as building 'biological software'. It uses deep learning to design mRNA and other RNA molecules for vaccines and therapeutics. Designed molecules are tested in the lab and licensed to pharma partners.
